rewrite.description: Microcosmos is a spacious cycle of cosmic country songs from Lou Turner, her warm, conversational voice finding humor and grace in small domestic moments. Its deadpan warmth recalls Silver Jews and Lambchop, for listeners who like country songs slow and wry.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to '70s singer-songwriters like Joni Mitchell, with touchstones in Bill Callahan and Silver Jews' wry, plainspoken style.

rewrite.description: Kate Bollinger's kaleidoscopic full-length debut ranges from homespun folk songs to warmly psychedelic rock. Her airy soprano and jazzy, organic arrangements give it a Laurel Canyon-adjacent glow.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to Françoise Hardy, the Velvet Underground and Teenage Fanclub as much as country, landing at the pop-facing edge of this lane's '70s revival strand.

rewrite.description: High Roller is an ornate, emotionally heavy solo record from Sima Cunningham, one half of Chicago's Finom (formerly Ohmme). It moves from spare piano balladry to fuller arrangements, her clear voice carrying songs of grief and devotion.
rewrite.lineage: A solo outlet for a Chicago DIY-scene fixture and Finom member, trading that band's angular guitars for piano-led songwriting.

rewrite.description: I'm Green is Mali Velasquez's folk-inflected indie rock debut, swinging between hushed verses and explosive choruses. Her plainspoken lyrics and warm voice place her alongside a wave of songwriters bridging bedroom folk and full-band indie rock.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds close to Katy Kirby, working the space between quiet acoustic folk and full-band indie rock.

rewrite.description: Green World is lush, adventurous folk from Adrian O'Barr's Wildflower, with pedal steel, saxophone, violin and harmonies woven into ample twang. Songs about coastlines and long drives make it a warm, springlike record built for the open road.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds like jazz-minded, twangy folk-rock from this lane's more pastoral end.

rewrite.description: Pirate Ship Playground is tasteful dual-vocal folk that recalls mid-2000s indie folk without tipping into twee. It favors close harmony, soft acoustic guitars and warmth over ornament.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds close to the soft-spoken folk-rock of the Burlington, Vermont scene around Greg Freeman.

rewrite.description: Neighbors is Meredith Nesbitt's Shoulderbird record, modest, intimate folksy Midwest Americana about moving, displacement and holding onto family. It favors plainspoken detail over ornament, with soft acoustic guitars and gentle harmonies.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds of a piece with Chicago's hushed folk-rock network.

rewrite.description: Rooftops in the Centerfold is Will Lawrence's understated record of dusky, nostalgic folk-rock about love, loss and the natural world. It mines a tasteful, unhurried palette of warm guitars and soft vocals, for listeners who like their folk-rock quiet and autumnal.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds of a piece with the patient, small-town-focused strand of indie folk around Itasca and Jess Williamson.

rewrite.description: My Bloody Valentine's debut full-length trades their earlier jangle-pop for tremolo-bent, detuned guitars smeared into a single churning mass, with Bilinda Butcher and Kevin Shields' vocals buried as texture rather than lead instrument. It lays out the template later shoegaze bands built on: pitch-bending 'glide guitar,' whispered half-heard lyrics, drums pushed flat into the mix. For listeners who want to hear the style before Loveless perfected it.

problems: lineage mixes documented scene with inferred Wednesday link

rewrite.description: Loveless buries impossibly detuned, whammy-bar-warped guitars, cooing dual vocals and a hidden pop core under layers of studio experimentation. It is the canonical entry for the guitar-wall vocabulary, the 'noise wall' and 'harmonized guitars' that countrygaze bands filter through pedal steel decades later. Essential listening for anyone tracing where the fuzz-and-drone side of the atlas gets its sonic palette.
rewrite.lineage: The aesthetic peak of the shoegaze branch off V29's drone lineage; its guitar-wall production sounds like a source for the noise/slowcore Context lane and, at a distance, the pedal-steel-and-fuzz textures of Core countrygaze bands like Wednesday.

problems: lineage mixes documented scene with inferred echoes

rewrite.description: Slowdive slow their guitars down from My Bloody Valentine's roar into something closer to ambient music, with Neil Halstead and Rachel Goswell's voices floating over reverb-drenched chords and Brian Eno contributing to 'Sing.' It softened shoegaze into dream pop proper. A key listen for hearing the gentler, more melodic half of the guitar-wall lineage.

problems: lineage mixes documented scene with inferred direction

rewrite.lineage: Part of the same Creation-label shoegaze scene as My Bloody Valentine; its more melodic, jangle-inflected guitar wall seems to point toward Britpop's guitar bands rather than back toward the Core's twang.

problems: lineage mixes documented scene with inferred drift

rewrite.description: A cleaner, more confident follow-up to Nowhere, Going Blank Again opens with the widescreen 'Leave Them All Behind' and leans further into pop hooks without losing the guitar haze. It is Ride at their most expansive before Britpop swept shoegaze aside. Useful for tracing how the genre's guitar-wall vocabulary bent toward more conventional rock structure.
rewrite.lineage: Continues Ride's place in the Creation-label shoegaze scene; its arena-ready hooks show the guitar-wall aesthetic drifting toward mainstream British guitar rock rather than the DIY/Core lineage.

rewrite.description: Elizabeth Fraser's wordless, glossolalia-like vocals float over Robin Guthrie's chiming, reverb-soaked guitar and synth washes, defining the ethereal 4AD sound years before shoegaze proper existed. Treasure is often treated as a founding dream-pop text and a clear antecedent for the vocal-as-texture approach shoegaze bands adopted. A landmark for the 'cosmic' and 'hushed' end of the guitar-wall vocabulary.
rewrite.lineage: An earlier, vocal-forward ancestor of the shoegaze branch off V29's drone lineage; its atmosphere prefigures My Bloody Valentine and Slowdive, and Slowdive in particular have acknowledged the band as an influence.

rewrite.description: Sonic Youth-style tunings and My Bloody Valentine-like guitar haze get filtered through American college-rock scrappiness, with tape loops, drum-machine interludes and sudden noise collages spliced between the pop songs. It is a landmark of American shoegaze and sounds like a forerunner of the lo-fi, guitar-wall indie that later feeds countrygaze's noisier edges.
rewrite.lineage: Transplants the UK shoegaze branch of V29 into the Boston DIY/college-radio network; its noisy, tape-collaged version of the guitar wall sounds closer to American noise-pop and lo-fi than to the UK dream-pop line.

rewrite.description: Mission of Burma's only studio album from their original run pairs blaring, tape-loop-treated guitar squall with tightly wound rhythms and Roger Miller and Clint Conley's alternating shouted vocals. It is a foundational text for American noise-rock and post-hardcore. Essential for the angular, rhythmic line that runs from Boston's scene through Fugazi and beyond.
rewrite.lineage: An American, Boston-scene branch off X14's punk foundation and V29's art-noise lineage; its tape-loop noise and structural aggression sound like groundwork for the noise-rock wing of X10 rather than any twang-adjacent lane.

problems: lineage timeline backwards (SST network predates Fugazi)

rewrite.description: Fugazi's first full-length turns Ian MacKaye's hardcore background and Guy Picciotto's more melodic instincts into tense, dub-influenced post-hardcore built on stop-start dynamics and pointedly political lyrics. Repeater made the band's DIY ethics (five-dollar shows, no merch) as influential as its music. The essential landmark for the DIY-network end of the rhythmic, angular line.
rewrite.lineage: Grows out of X14's hardcore-punk roots (MacKaye's earlier Minor Threat) with an art-rock structural sense that recalls V29; Fugazi's DIY model became a touchstone for the independent touring network that runs into lo-fi indie and the Core.

rewrite.description: A heavier, more abrasive record than Repeater, In on the Kill Taker came together after the band shelved early sessions with Steve Albini and finished it on their own terms. It holds some of Fugazi's most aggressive material and shows the post-hardcore/noise-rock overlap within the lane at its most direct. A strong second landmark for the band's catalog.
rewrite.lineage: Continues Fugazi's post-hardcore branch, with abandoned Albini sessions brushing it against the noise-rock wing of the same lane; its aggression seems to have shaped 90s post-hardcore more than any twang-adjacent lineage.

rewrite.description: Fugazi loosen their sound on Red Medicine, adding studio experimentation, instrumental detours and quieter passages alongside the usual tense dynamics, self-produced entirely on their own terms. It shows a band expanding past hardcore's constraints while keeping its DIY politics intact. Recommended for hearing the band's mid-career evolution.

rewrite.description: Protomartyr's fourth album widens its scope to post-truth politics and mortality, with Casey's lyrics sharper and the band's arrangements more expansive than on earlier records. Ahee's guitars shift between spindly patterns and heavy surges under the baritone narration. Recommended as a second, more polished entry point.
rewrite.lineage: Continues Protomartyr's modern post-punk branch off X14/V29; its political storytelling parallels Southern-gothic songwriting elsewhere in the atlas without ever crossing into twang.

rewrite.description: Blackberry Smoke's Rounder Records debut straddles rock radio and Nashville without softening its boogie-rock core, with twin guitars, organ and Charlie Starr's warm drawl. It shows Southern rock's mainstream continuation as a working, touring band rather than a nostalgia act. A solid second landmark for the band's arc.
rewrite.lineage: Continues Blackberry Smoke's branch off V28's Southern-rock lineage into commercial country-rock crossover, far from the Core's indie/DIY route.

problems: lineage is trajectory, not documented link

rewrite.description: Mud pairs Whiskey Myers' Skynyrd-indebted riffing with more polished, radio-ready production and big, gang-sung choruses. It marks the point where the band's Southern-rock revival sound became fully arena-ready. A useful landmark for the lane's commercial peak.
rewrite.lineage: A polished entry in Whiskey Myers' branch off V28's Southern-rock lineage, aimed at mainstream rock-radio and streaming audiences rather than the DIY/indie route.

rewrite.description: Formed by the sons of three founding Allman Brothers Band members (Devon Allman, Duane Betts, Berry Duane Oakley), the Allman Betts Band's debut revives the twin-lead-guitar, jam-friendly sound of their fathers' band. It is the most literal possible continuation of Southern rock's original lineage into the present. Essential for showing the mainstream continuation as a direct family inheritance.

Bless Your Heart stretches into longer, more improvisational arrangements than the debut, closer to the Allman Brothers' live-jam tradition. It doubles down on the band's role as caretakers of their fathers' sound rather than pushing toward reinvention. Recommended as a second, jammier landmark.

problems: lineage influence citations unsupported; mix of documented cover and resemblance

rewrite.lineage: Extends V28's Southern-rock lineage through a heavier outlaw-country filter that sounds indebted to Waylon Jennings and Skynyrd, backed by its David Allan Coe cover; closer to the Core's storytelling instincts than most of this lane but still landing in mainstream rock/Americana touring rather than indie twang.
